title: Formative Assessment: Definitions and Relationships
extended_summary:
This paper addresses a conceptual problem in the assessment literature: the lack of agreement about what counts as formative assessment and how it differs from related ideas such as feedback, assessment for learning, and assessment of learning. Wiliam reviews the historical origins of feedback and formative assessment, arguing that effective assessment must be understood as part of a broader instructional system rather than as a standalone intervention. The paper synthesizes findings from earlier reviews and meta-analyses to show that feedback can improve learning, but only when it is used by teachers and/or students to change subsequent instructional or learning activity.

The paper does not report a single new empirical intervention. Instead, it analyzes a wide range of prior research spanning elementary, middle, high school, and college-aged learners, with especially strong attention to K-12 classroom assessment. It discusses classroom feedback practices, teacher use of assessment data, student self-assessment, and systems of formative assessment embedded in instruction. The paper also notes subject-specific examples, including mathematics, reading, history, figurative language, and chemistry, to illustrate how feedback must be domain-specific and tied to the learning task.

The main conclusion is that formative assessment should be defined by whether evidence is actually used to adapt teaching to student needs, not merely by the collection of information about student performance. Wiliam emphasizes that effective formative assessment depends on the learning milieu, teacher responses, and student responses, and that simple feedback or grades alone are often insufficient. The paper concludes that classroom-level reform in formative assessment is central rather than marginal and will require sustained support, but it does not identify a single best model for practice.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring system or related instructional feedback system that provides adaptive guidance, feedback, or assessment support within a learning environment.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses formative assessment and feedback as general instructional concepts and reviews evidence from feedback/assessment systems, but it does not study a specific AI product or generative AI tool.

findings.finding_summary: Across prior research on formative assessment and feedback, the paper reports that effective classroom assessment can improve student achievement, with reviews finding effects typically around 0.4 to 0.7 standard deviations. The paper also notes that feedback is more effective when it is task-focused, timely, and used to adapt instruction, rather than merely providing grades or praise.
findings.measure: Student achievement / learning outcomes in classroom assessment and feedback studies
findings.effect_size: 0.4 to 0.7 SD (reviewed literature); also 0.32 SD in one classroom implementation cited

quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/review paper about formative assessment and feedback, not an empirical evaluation of a specific AI tool. It synthesizes prior literature rather than reporting a new controlled study of an instructional AI system.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper summarizes moderate positive effects reported in prior research on formative assessment (often above 0.20 SD), but these are not findings about a specific AI tool in this paper. The direct evidence for the paper itself is therefore not tool-specific and remains indirect.
